core.text: To say whose something is, Latin puts the owner into **the genitive (the 'of' form)**, *genitīvus possessīvus*: *fīlius Iūliī* = the son of Julius, Julius's son; *ancilla Aemiliae* = Aemilia's maid. Owner and thing owned need not stand side by side; the ending shows the link. The question word is *cuius?* (whose?).
English shows possession with *'s* or *of*: *the man's house*, *the roof of the house*. Latin uses one ending for both and no *of*.
The owner takes the genitive: singular -ae (a-nouns), -ī (us- and um-nouns); plural -ārum, -ōrum. It may stand before or after the noun it belongs to.

invented.en: The master's stick is in the garden.

core.text: *Puellae* is the genitive (of the girl) and also the dative (the 'to/for' form), to the girl; *servī* is genitive singular (of the slave) and nominative plural (slaves). Look at the neighbours: a genitive hangs on another noun (*liber puellae* — the girl's book); a dative hangs on a verb of giving (*puellae librum dat* — gives the girl a book).

teach.title: Whose?

notice.ask: Tap the word in each sentence that says whose. What tail do the two share?

teach.say: The owner stands in the genitive (the 'of' form): Latin says whose something is by changing the owner’s ending instead of adding a word. The question it answers is *cuius?*, whose? *Iūlius pater Quīntī et Mārcī est* — Julius is the father of Quintus and Marcus.

teach.title: a-nouns: -ae
teach.say: An a-noun makes this form by turning -a into -ae: *domina* (mistress) becomes *dominae*, of the mistress. So *ancilla dominae* is the mistress’s slave girl.

teach.title: us-nouns and um-nouns: -ī
teach.say: *Dominus* (master) becomes *dominī*, and *capitulum* (chapter) becomes *capitulī*: both groups take the same tail, -ī. So *servus dominī* is the master’s slave and *titulus capitulī* the chapter’s title.

teach.title: Several owners: -ōrum, and -ārum for a-nouns
teach.say: When the owners are more than one the tail grows: us- and um-nouns take -ōrum (*puerōrum*, of the boys) and a-nouns -ārum (*puellārum*, of the girls). *Pater puerōrum* is the boys’ father, *māter puellārum* the girls’ mother. The us-noun’s cell is filled in for you; the a-noun’s is the one to write.

teach.title: The owner may stand on either side
teach.say: *Mārcī pater* and *pater Mārcī* both mean Marcus’s father, and another word may even come between the two. Latin does not fix the order, because the ending has already done the work. Find the -ae or -ī word, then ask which noun it belongs to.

teach.title: -ae and -ī also make plurals
teach.say: *Ancillae* is ‘slave girls’ and *Aemiliae* is ‘of Aemilia’, and they end alike; so do *servī* (slaves) and *dominī* (of the master). An owner hangs on another noun, so ask which of the two the other belongs to. *Ancillae Aemiliae in familiā sunt*: Aemilia is one person, so *Aemiliae* is the owner.

more.text: From the learner's notes: grammatical 'possession' is broad. It covers holding something (the student's library book), owning it (my book on your shelf), and simply a close tie (the man's wife). English pronouns still have a genitive (*his*, *her*, *whose*), and English always puts the possessor first; Latin may put it either side of its noun and even split the two with another word (*pānēs sunt fēminae*).

Ørberg cap. II: genetīvus -ī / -ōrum for masculine and neuter, -ae / -ārum for feminine, with the question *cuius?*. Names in -ius have genitive -iī (*Iūliī*), often written with one ī. For 'my', 'your', 'his own' Latin does not use a genitive but the adjectives *meus*, *tuus*, *suus*, which agree with the thing owned: *servus meus*, *ancilla tua*. For 'his' meaning someone else's it uses *eius*. A&G §343.
English has two ways to say it, *Marcus’s father* and *the father of Marcus*; Latin has one ending for both and no word for ‘of’.
Then the verb confirms it: *Ancillae Aemiliae in familiā sunt* has *sunt*, and only *ancillae* can be the several ones, because Aemilia is one person.
